mainEntity.name: How do I know if my tooth wear is severe enough to need a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is something a dentist will assess during a clinical examination. They will evaluate how much tooth structure has been lost, whether dentine is exposed, and whether the tooth is at risk of fracture. Mild wear may not require immediate restorative treatment, while more advanced cases may benefit from a crown to protect the remaining structure. Regular check-ups allow wear to be monitored over time, so decisions can be made at the appropriate stage.

mainEntity.name: Can a crown be placed on a tooth that is still sensitive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sensitivity is a common symptom of tooth wear, particularly when dentine is exposed. In many cases, sensitivity resolves once the tooth is covered with a crown, as it seals the dentinal tubules. However, if sensitivity is severe or related to pulp involvement, a dentist will assess whether additional treatment — such as root canal therapy — is needed before crown placement. Each case is assessed individually.

mainEntity.name: How long does a dental crown last on a worn tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Crown longevity varies depending on the material used, the patient's bite, oral hygiene, and whether the cause of wear has been managed. In general, well-maintained crowns can last ten years or more, and many last considerably longer. If bruxism is a contributing factor and is left unmanaged, crowns may wear or fracture more quickly, which is why occlusal splints are often recommended alongside restorative work.
Patients with concerns about long-term durability may also find this helpful: can a crown stop your tooth from cracking?

mainEntity.name: Will I need a crown on every tooth affected by wear?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. The need for crowns on specific teeth depends on the severity of wear and the risk to each individual tooth. Some teeth may require crowns while others can be managed with composite bonding, preventative measures, or simply monitoring. A comprehensive treatment plan will be developed based on a thorough assessment of all affected teeth, prioritising those most at risk.

mainEntity.name: Is tooth wear treatment available on the NHS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some restorative treatment for tooth wear may be available on the NHS, particularly where it is clinically necessary. However, certain materials and techniques — such as porcelain or zirconia crowns — may only be available privately, as NHS treatment follows specific material guidelines. A dentist will be able to advise on what options are available to you based on your individual circumstances and treatment needs.

mainEntity.name: Can I prevent tooth wear from getting worse without treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, yes — particularly where the wear is mild and the contributing cause has been identified and addressed. Modifying dietary habits, improving brushing technique, wearing an occlusal splint for bruxism, and attending regular check-ups can all help reduce the rate of further wear. However, where significant wear has already occurred, professional restorative treatment is often the most effective way to protect the tooth from further damage.
